faq.a: No, it is non‑invasive; dysentery suggests E. histolytica or another pathogen.
No treatment is required; focus on hygiene and safe water.
faq.q: Do I need to treat an asymptomatic patient with cysts on stool microscopy?

faq.a: PCR or a specific E. histolytica antigen test; microscopy cannot differentiate.
faq.q: What is the best test to differentiate E. dispar from E. histolytica?

exam: A 25‑year‑old farmer presents with mild abdominal discomfort and cysts on stool microscopy. What is your next step? — Assess symptoms; if no dysentery or liver signs, no anti‑amoebic therapy, advise hygiene.

In a patient with bloody diarrhoea and liver abscess, stool shows Entamoeba cysts. How do you confirm the pathogen? — Order E. histolytica‑specific antigen test or PCR; treat presumptively if unavailable.
Why is metronidazole avoided in an asymptomatic patient with only E. dispar cysts? — It treats invasive disease; unnecessary exposure risks side‑effects and resistance.
What public‑health measures reduce Entamoeba transmission in low‑resource settings? — Safe water, latrine use, hand‑washing, food hygiene.
How would you explain the difference between E. dispar and E. histolytica to a patient? — One lives harmlessly in the gut, the other can invade tissue and cause serious illness.

A HIV‑positive patient has chronic diarrhoea; stool microscopy shows Entamoeba cysts. What additional investigations are warranted? — Rule out E. histolytica with antigen test/PCR and consider other opportunistic pathogens.
ai.title: Entamoeba dispar Infection
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Entamoeba dispar is a non‑invasive intestinal amoeba that mimics E. histolytica on microscopy but does not cause disease. Recognising it prevents unnecessary treatment in low‑resource settings.

b: Transmission: fecal‑oral via cysts in contaminated water/food
Epidemiology: common in East Africa, South Asia, Latin America
Clinical significance: usually asymptomatic, may cause mild abdominal discomfort
sections.p: Entamoeba dispar is a commensal protozoan found worldwide, especially in areas with poor sanitation. It is morphologically identical to the pathogenic E. histolytica, so diagnosis relies on molecular or antigen tests.

b: PCR or antigen detection required for definitive differentiation
Presence of cysts alone does not imply disease
sections.p: Distinguish E. dispar from E. histolytica to avoid overtreatment. In low‑resource hospitals, clinical suspicion is low; focus on epidemiology and simple stool microscopy, then decide if further testing is needed.

b: Consider E. dispar when stool shows cysts but patient lacks dysentery, fever, or liver lesions
In HIV or malnourished patients, still prioritize ruling out E. histolytica
sections.p: Patients rarely need therapy, but misdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary metronidazole use, contributing to resistance and side‑effects. Recognise when to investigate further, especially in patients with dysentery or liver abscess where E. histolytica is more likely.
When PCR or antigen kits are unavailable, treat only if clinical picture suggests invasive disease (e.g., bloody diarrhea, liver abscess).

t.b: Are cysts or trophozoites present? – Confirms Entamoeba spp. but cannot separate species

t.a: Rapid antigen test (e.g., ELISA for E. histolytica antigen)
t.b: Is the antigen specific for E. histolytica positive? – Positive means pathogenic infection; negative suggests E. dispar or other non‑pathogenic species
Does the DNA match E. dispar or E. histolytica? – Definitive species identification; guides treatment decision

b: Re‑hydrate if diarrhoea present – oral rehydration salts
Educate on hand‑washing, boiling water, proper food handling
Avoid metronidazole unless invasive disease is likely
sections.p: No anti‑amoebic therapy is required for asymptomatic E. dispar infection. Focus on hygiene education and safe water. If co‑infection with E. histolytica is suspected, give metronidazole followed by a luminal agent.

b: E. histolytica: bloody stools, fever, hepatic lesions
Giardia: foul‑smelling, fatty stools, no liver involvement
sections.p: Entamoeba histolytica – invasive, causes dysentery, liver abscess; requires metronidazole. Giardia lamblia – causes greasy stools, diagnosed by trophozoite/cyst morphology distinct from Entamoeba.

b: Negative antigen test in low‑resource labs → may miss rare invasive cases
sections.p: Microscopy alone may over‑diagnose invasive disease, leading to unnecessary treatment. Antigen tests that detect only E. histolytica can miss co‑infection with E. dispar, but this is clinically irrelevant.

b: Key question: Is the patient symptomatic with signs of invasive amoebiasis?
Remember: E. dispar = no tissue invasion
sections.p: Focus on differentiation strategies, epidemiology, and when to treat.

whenToSeekHelp: High‑grade fever, severe abdominal pain, or signs of liver abscess in a patient with Entamoeba cysts – urgent referral for imaging and possible anti‑amoebic therapy
